clinicalScope: Cytokines in the context of infectious and inflammatory disease in low‑resource, East African hospitals
title: Cytokines in Infectious and Inflammatory Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: Cytokines are tiny proteins that act as messengers during infection and inflammation. In low‑resource settings they drive the severity of sepsis, malaria, TB and HIV complications, guiding diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.

sections.p: Cytokines are small proteins secreted by immune cells that modulate inflammation and immune responses. In East Africa, they are key mediators of severe infections such as sepsis, malaria, TB and HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
b: Small proteins (5–20 kDa) produced by leukocytes, endothelial cells and others
Act locally or systemically to recruit cells, activate inflammation
Elevated levels correlate with disease severity in sepsis, malaria, TB

t.b: High in severe malaria and sepsis; >10 pg/mL indicates poor prognosis

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, cytokine storms are most often triggered by infections that are common and untreated.
b: Bacterial sepsis (pneumonia, meningitis, urinary tract infection)
Herbal remedies that provoke immune activation

sections.p: Cytokines orchestrate a cascade that increases vascular permeability, recruits immune cells and activates coagulation, leading to organ dysfunction.
b: IL‑1, IL‑6, TNF‑α stimulate endothelial cells to express adhesion molecules
Endothelial glycocalyx degradation increases capillary leak
Coagulation activation leads to microthrombi and organ ischemia

sections.p: Clinical features reflect systemic inflammation and organ dysfunction driven by cytokines.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: History focuses on infection source, recent travel, HIV status and herbal use. Examination looks for signs of capillary leak and organ dysfunction.
b: Ask about fever pattern, cough, dysuria, recent insect bites
Check for HIV status, TB exposure, malaria endemicity
Assess capillary refill, skin turgor, oedema
Look for JVD, ascites, pleural rubs, lung crackles

sections.p: Conditions that mimic cytokine‑driven inflammation but have different underlying causes.
b: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Tests are chosen to confirm infection, assess organ function and guide therapy. Availability may be limited.
Severity is graded using the SOFA score and lactate levels, guiding escalation of care.
Co‑morbidities and resource limits can mask or mimic cytokine effects.
b: Antibiotic overuse can alter culture results

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support organ function and monitor cytokine‑driven complications.
b: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids (30 mL/kg bolus)

t.b: Crystalloids preferred over colloids in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Early recognition of organ failure prevents mortality.

t.b: Consider mechanical ventilation if SpO₂ <90% on oxygen

b: Children – lower fluid tolerance, higher infection risk

t.b: Avoid teratogenic drugs; use ceftriaxone safely

sections.p: Prognosis depends on early recognition and resource availability. Prevention focuses on infection control and vaccination.
b: Mortality 30–50% in severe sepsis without ICU
Regular monitoring of vitals and urine output
Prompt malaria prophylaxis in endemic areas

sections.p: Certain tests may give false negatives or positives in low‑resource settings.
b: Blood cultures may be negative if antibiotics started early
Rapid malaria tests may miss low parasitemia
CRP can be normal in early sepsis or in malnourished patients

t.b: Confirm with microscopy if clinical picture fits

sections.p: Other conditions that share systemic inflammation but differ in pathogenesis.
b: Severe bacterial sepsis vs. viral sepsis – viral lacks neutrophilia
Malaria vs. dengue – dengue has thrombocytopenia, plasma leakage
Sickle cell crisis vs. infection – crisis has pain crisis, no fever

t.b: Painful vaso‑occlusive episodes, no systemic cytokine surge

faq.q: What is the main role of IL‑6 in sepsis?
faq.a: IL‑6 drives acute‑phase response, fever, and vascular permeability, contributing to organ dysfunction.

faq.q: Why avoid NSAIDs in septic patients?
faq.a: NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion and increase bleeding risk in coagulopathy.

faq.q: When is a blood culture negative but sepsis still likely?
faq.a: If antibiotics were started before sampling, or in early sepsis with low bacterial load.

exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected septic shock in a low‑resource setting? — Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics and give a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus; monitor MAP and lactate.
Which cytokine is most useful as a prognostic marker in severe malaria? — IL‑6; levels >10 pg/mL predict mortality.
Why is norepinephrine preferred over dopamine in septic shock? — Norepinephrine has less arrhythmogenicity and better MAP maintenance.
What laboratory finding would prompt you to suspect DIC in a septic patient? — INR >1.5 with platelets <50k/µL.
How would you differentiate malaria from dengue in a febrile patient with thrombocytopenia? — Dengue shows platelets <100k/µL, abdominal pain, plasma leakage; malaria shows parasitemia on smear.
When should you consider mechanical ventilation in a patient with cytokine‑mediated respiratory failure? — SpO₂ <90% on 100% O₂ or PaO₂/FiO₂ <200.
What is the rationale for avoiding NSAIDs in a patient with sepsis and AKI? — NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal perfusion, worsening AKI.
Which infection is most likely to cause a cytokine storm in an HIV‑positive patient in East Africa? — Cryptococcal meningitis or TB meningitis.
How does endothelial glycocalyx degradation contribute to capillary leak? — It removes the barrier, allowing plasma proteins and fluid to escape into interstitium.
What is the significance of a lactate >4 mmol/L in a septic patient? — It indicates severe hypoperfusion and predicts higher mortality.
